title: Gene structure and frequencies across populations

segs.text: Section seven. Gene structure and frequencies across populations. The first figure shows where in a gene variants occur. The promoter is where the machinery for expressing the gene starts. Exons are the D N A that ends up as amino acid sequence. Introns were once thought meaningless, but variations occur there too. A stop codon sits at the end. Variants are sorted into those changing protein abundance, those changing the protein product, and markers for nearby or distant functional variation.

The second figure shows that allele and phenotype frequencies differ widely between populations. For C Y P three A five, star one is the wild type and star three, six and seven are non-functional. In sub-Saharan African populations star one is common and all three variants are present; in European populations few alleles are wild type, and most are star three.

For V K O R C one minus sixteen thirty nine, G to A, the G allele means a higher dose is required and the A allele a lower dose, compared across African, European and North American, and East Asian populations. For T P M T, most people are normal metabolizers, with only a small bar of poor metabolizers.

Frequency together with severity of the toxicity decides how much to worry about a variant, including whether to genotype a whole population. Azathioprine and six mercaptopurine are metabolized by T P M T. Few people are T P M T poor metabolizers, but one given the normal dose could die; they need less than ten percent of the normal dose. So a rare phenotype can still justify genotyping when the toxicity is severe.
